description: ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the Fourth theme, Suitability and Attainable Yield, is displayed here. It combines multiple inputs ranging from climatic conditions, water supply, and agricultural input levels to spatially map the suitability of 4 different crops globally. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616). ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources are important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on current crop suitability and assess its potential impact from climate change. Coffee, Cotton, Dryland Rice, and Wetland Rice are important commodities around the globe and the Crop Suitability Class provides important spatial information on where these commodities will thrive or face challenges in future timeframes and under different climate scenarios. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data is derived from multiple climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Suitability Class sub-theme falls under Theme Four of the outputs and Module V of the modeling framework. Module V integrates results from the first four modules and combines agro-climatic potential yields with soil and terrain evaluation results. This Module identifies in each grid cell its respective soil types and slope classes and then assesses and assigns a suitability rating and simulated potential yield. Results are then aggregated and mapped for each historic and future 30-year period by crop, input level, and water source and have a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). Suitability classes are calculated from the normalized Suitability Index (SI), where: SI = 100 x (90 x VS + 70 x S + 50 x MS + 30 x mS + 15 x VmS + 0 x NS) / 0.9 SI values can range from 0 to 10,000 and the acronyms that are underlying suitability classes are defined as follows: VS = very suitable, S = suitable, MS = moderately suitable, mS = marginally suitable, VmS = very marginally suitable, and NS = not suitable. These six categories represent the shares of area extents of the different suitability classes in a grid cell. SI is calculated for each of the 53 crops by the level of input, management, and water supply system. The resultant SI in each grid cell is then grouped into eight classes depicting the aggregate crop suitability as: - Very high: SI > 8,500 - High: 7,000 < SI ≤ 8,500 - Good: 5,550 < SI ≤ 7,000 - Medium: 4,000 < SI ≤ 5,500 - Moderate: 2,500 < SI ≤ 4,000 - Marginal: 1,000 < SI ≤ 2,500 - Very marginal: 0 < SI ≤ 1,000 - Not suitable: SI = 0 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Crop Suitability Index full dataset has data for 53 crops, additional timeframes (1961-1990, 1971-2000, and 2071-2100), RCPs (2.6 and 6.0), water supply (rainfed all phases, gravity irrigation), a low input level option, and a without CO2 fertilization option. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_067_rw0_crop_suitability_class). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Food from the Sea dataset on Resource Watch presents a record of the production, import, export, caloric supply, and protein supply from ocean-sourced food (also known as ‘blue food’) in a country’s food supply from 1961 to 2018. This indicator takes into account marine plants and animals as well as their processed food derivatives and is measured in kilocalories per person per day. This data comes from the Food Balance Sheets produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and is aggregated by the Resource Watch team to sum all ocean-derived food commodities. Fish and plant production from the sea has increased over time, providing an important food source for many across the globe. Although fish provided an average of only about 35 calories per capita per day in 2017, according to the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/ca9229en/ca9229en.pdf), fish play an important role in global food provision, accounting for about 17 percent of animal protein and 7 percent of all protein consumed by humans. This number is even higher in some developing regions and many small island developing states, which derive 50 percent or more of their animal protein from aquatic foods. The ocean contributes a major portion of the world’s fish products, with ocean-based production representing nearly 90 percent of global landings from capture fisheries and about a third of aquaculture production. As the global population and people’s incomes rise, the demand for ocean-derived food will continue to grow. [By some estimates](http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/templates/wsfs/docs/expert_paper/How_to_Feed_the_World_in_2050.pdf), nearly 500 million metric tons of animal meat will be required to feed the global population in 2050. Because of its reduced impact on climate change, feed efficiency, production potential, nutrition, and accessibility, food from the sea [has a large potential to meet this need](https://oceanpanel.org/sites/default/files/2019-11/19_HLP_BP1%20Paper.pdf). The FAO Food Balance Sheets (FBS) present a comprehensive and consolidated resource for assessing the pattern of a country’s food supply and its utilization on an annual basis. The FBS data are generally used to support policy analysis and decision-making, to provide an assessment of self-sufficiency, to estimate whether nutritional requirements are met, and as a major element for projection of food demand. For fish and fish products, they also represent a useful tool to monitor the development in overall domestic fish availability and utilization, reveal changes in the types of species consumed, and give an indication of the role of fish in total food supply and its share in animal and overall proteins. ### Methodology Food Balance Sheets (FBS) are compiled every year by FAO, mainly with country-level data on the production and trade of food commodities. Using this data and the available information on loss coefficients, stock changes, and types of utilization, available food supplies are calculated. This is achieved by taking domestic production (capture fisheries and aquaculture), minus non-food uses, minus exports, plus imports, plus or minus variation in stocks. Specific food composition factors are then applied to the related supply of each product type in order to obtain calories, proteins and fats. In order to have comparable statistics applicable to all countries in the world, data are then converted into primary equivalent (live weight equivalent, i.e. the weight of the fish at the time of harvest) using specific technical conversion factors. The per capita supply of each item available for human consumption is then obtained by dividing the respective quantity by the resident population. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://fenixservices.fao.org/faostat/static/documents/FBS/New%20FBS%20methodology.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for other commodities and food supply components as well as the full time series are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The FAO Food Balance Sheet data was aggregated by the Resource Watch team by summing the total dietary energy supply coming from ocean-derived food commodities by country. The FAO Food Balance Sheet categories that were considered ocean-derived food commodities and summed include: Demersal Fish (2762); Pelagic Fish (2763); Marine Fish, Other (2764); Crustaceans (2765); Cephalopods (2766); Molluscs, Other (2767); Meat, Aquatic Mammals (2768); Aquatic Animals, Others (2769); Aquatic Plants (2775); Fish, Body Oil (2781); and Fish, Liver Oil (2782). See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_061_rw0_blue_food_supply). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata and the [The Future of Food from the Sea Blue Paper](https://oceanpanel.org/sites/default/files/2019-11/19_HLP_BP1%20Paper.pdf) commissioned by the High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy.

GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). description: The Ecological Footprint of Consumption data set, released by the Global Footprint Network, defines the area used to support a defined population’s consumption. The consumption Footprint in global hectares (ha) includes the area needed to produce the materials consumed and the area needed to absorb the carbon dioxide emissions. The consumption footprint of a nation is calculated in the National Footprint Accounts as a nation’s primary production footprint plus the footprint of imports minus the footprint of exports, and is thus, strictly speaking, a footprint of apparent consumption. The national average of per capita consumption footprint is equal to a country’s consumption footprint divided by its population. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. As nations urbanize and citizens become wealthier, people generally increase the share of resource-intensive foods—such as meats and dairy—in their diets. Although some of this shift reflects health and welfare gains for many people, shifts to high-meat diets will make it harder for the world to achieve several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including those on hunger, healthy lives, water management, climate change, and terrestrial ecosystems. The availability of animal based foods data here represent retail-level availability of animal-based foods (meat, dairy, fish, eggs) per capita per day across the world, from 1961-2013, with a "business as usual" projection, RCP 8.5, out to 2050. Data for 1961-2013 are from FAO's Food Balance Sheets. Data for 2050 are from FAO's projection of food demand and production. Because FAO projects that sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia in 2050 will still have insufficient calories to feed everyone adequately, WRI adjusted food amounts upward in those two regions to ensure 3,000 calories are available per person per day in all regions. Data for 2014-2050 are linear interpolations between observed (2013) and projected (2050) data. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). WHYMAP’s goal is to collect, combine and visualize global hydrogeological data to raise awareness of groundwater resources and promote global discussion on water issues. The Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates Map is a global map of groundwater resources at a scale of 1:25,000,000 and is used to characterize major groundwater environments and recharge rates. The maps used to characterize groundwater environments were selected by evaluating national, regional and continental maps at scales of 1:1,000,000 to 1:15,000,000. Maps at each of these scales were examined to develop continental maps at a scale of 1:10,000,000, which could then be combined into a global map. Differences in each map’s level of detail, philosophy, approach, hydrogeological interpretation and projection had to be considered when combining these maps. These maps were reviewed and redrawn to improve the consistency of methods for each continent. Hydrogeological mapping experts from different parts of the world contributed their regional knowledge to the final revision of these continental maps before they were combined into a final global map. Groundwater recharge rates represent the years 1961-1990. These values are derived from simulations with the global hydrological model WaterGAP, version 2.1f from the University of Frankfurt/Main, Germany. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: ### Overview The Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset shows the percentage of the population living below a $3.20 a day poverty line in 2011 international prices. The $3.20 poverty line is derived from typical national poverty lines in countries classified as Lower Middle Income. The dataset is created by comparing the $3.20 poverty line to income and consumption data from each country. Income and consumption data allows researchers to determine the cost of living and the cost of goods and services in each country based on 2011 pricing. This is used to convert the $3.20 poverty line into local currencies and poverty rates. The dataset is published for low- and middle-income countries, countries eligible to receive World Bank loans, and recently graduated countries only. It is available for all years from 1967-present and has a national spatial resolution. The dataset was created by the World Bank as part of its internationally comparable poverty monitoring database. The database serves to monitor poverty rates for all countries and utilizes different poverty rates for different country income classifications. The World Bank Group is committed to reducing extreme poverty to 3 percent or less, globally, by 2030. Monitoring poverty is important on the global development agenda as well as on the national development agenda of many countries. ### Methodology The Population below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset was created as part of the World Bank’s Poverty Measures of the Developing World database to calculate the poverty headcount ratio per country at a $3.20 a day poverty line. The poverty headcount ratio is the proportion of a population that lives below the poverty line. First, researchers determined the international poverty line to create a common standard of what “poverty” is. This was first done in the 1980’s by looking at academic papers on the economies of 22 developing countries and a poverty line of $1 a day was created. Since then new and updated international poverty lines have been created and as of 2015 the World Bank has used an international poverty line of $1.90 a day at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP). This was created by averaging the national poverty lines of 15 of the poorest countries ranked by per capita consumption. The dataset shown here uses a more liberal poverty line of $3.20, which is based on low- and middle- income countries. It is based on 2011 PPP, which means the monetary value is representative of the cost of specific goods in each country as of 2011 and highlights the differences in absolute purchasing power between economies. International poverty lines cannot be directly compared with poverty measured at national poverty lines in local currency, which reflect economy-specific decisions of poverty. To make them comparable and determine the rate of poverty in a country the international poverty line was applied to each country individually. To do this, income and consumption data from household surveys across 164 countries in six regions and 25 other high income countries were used to determine household living standards. The poverty line at 2011 PPP was converted into local currencies in 2011 prices and then converted to the prices of goods at the time of the relevant nationally representative household survey using the best available Consumer Price Index (CPI). CPI is a measure of the cost of consumer goods and services at a given time. Then the poverty rate was calculated by determining how much of the country's population fell below the $3.20 2011 PPP poverty line. The population living below the poverty line was then divided by the country’s total population and multiplied by 100 to create the final dataset. Nationally representative household surveys were conducted by national statistical offices or by private agencies under the supervision of government or international agencies and obtained from government statistical offices and World Bank Group operational departments. CPI data was primarily taken from the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) International Financial Statistics. To make national poverty rates comparable between countries they were calculated and shown for individual years, known as reference years. This required interpolating and extrapolating data for countries that lacked survey data for each year. This was done by adjusting the mean income or expenditure observed in a survey year by a country’s growth factor to estimate the unknown survey data in the reference year. For the full documentation, please see this [methodology document](http://iresearch.worldbank.org/PovcalNet/methodology.aspx) or click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Gini index measures economic inequality in a country. Specifically, it is the extent to which the distribution of income (or, in some cases, consumption expenditure) deviates from a perfectly equal distribution among individuals or households within an economy. A Gini index of 0 represents perfect equality, while an index of 100 implies perfect inequality. The Gini index dataset was released by the World Bank. This data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available for the years 1967-present, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. ### Methodology The Gini Index was calculated from the World Bank’s internationally comparable poverty monitoring database, which draws on income or detailed consumption data from more than 1,000 household surveys across 138 countries in 6 regions and 21 other high-income countries (industrialized economies). To calculate the Gini index, a Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, starting with the poorest individual or household. The Gini index measures the area between the Lorenz curve and a hypothetical (45-degree) line of absolute equality, expressed as a percentage of the maximum area under the line. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Global Material Flows Database holds a variety of datasets on material extraction and consumption. The dataset displayed on Resource Watch shows global material consumption and extraction of nonmetallic minerals, biomass, fossil fuels, and metal ores at a national scale. This data is available at the source for every year between 1970 and 2017, but only the 2017 data is mapped on Resource Watch. The dataset also contains additional data on the overall consumption and extraction for each country at a per capita rate for the year 2015. Consumption and extraction are expressed in units of metric tons. This dataset was created using national statistics from a combination of local government organizations and international organizations like the United Nations, Eurostat, and the United States Geological Survey. This dataset was developed to assist governments in creating strategies to increase efficiency of material production and consumption activities. The dataset can help in better understanding how economic growth patterns influence resource use. It can also be used to evaluate the impacts of policies that have been adopted in the past. Additionally, the dataset can be used to develop effective strategies to minimize future resource use through targeted consumption and production policies. This database is used by academics around the world, integrated into several multi-regional input-output databases such as [EXIOBASE](https://www.exiobase.eu/) and featured in reports by international organisations, such as the United Nations Environmental Program and the European Economic Area. This database was created by the United Nations Environment Programme International Resource Panel (UNEP IRP) and developed as part of a collaborative effort by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Sustainable Resource Use research group of the Vienna University of Economics and Business, the Institute of Social Ecology Vienna, the Nagoya University, and University of Sydney’s Integrated Sustainability Analysis. ### Methodology This dataset was created by combining data from multiple sources. Data for all categories of extraction were taken from national production statistics. These datasets were collected from individual government ministries, industrial associations, and Eurostat's production statistics (PRODCOM) whenever available. Additional available data from international organizations, like the British Geological Survey and United States Geological Survey, were also used. Some categories, like metal ore extraction, were estimated using techniques in the [Eurostat: Economy-wide Material Flow Accounts Compilation Guide 2013](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191533/2013-EW-MFA-Guide-10Sep2013.pdf/). Data reported using different units was converted to a standard unit by using category-specific conversion factors. Data on domestic material consumption was calculated by finding the sum of each country’s domestic extraction and import values and subtracting total exports. Data on imports and exports was taken from national offices when available and United Nations reports when not available. Both per capita datasets were created by dividing each country’s total extraction and consumption by its population. The final datasets were produced in tabular format at a national level. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for categories such as crops, natural gas and petroleum are available from the data provider. For each of these categories, data on trade, raw material consumption, raw material consumption per capita, raw material inputs, raw material equivalents of imports, raw material equivalents of exports is also provided. Lastly, data for each year from 1970 to 2017 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](72607dcf-8876-489c-94f2-28e9e10208bc) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows potential climate change impacts on world crop production and yield from 1970-2000 to 2080 under different emissions scenarios. The impact under different emissions scenarios is reported as the percentage change from this baseline. This dataset includes the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. This dataset is an update to a major crop modeling study by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). ### Methodology The initial study was published in 1997, based on output of the HadCM2 model forced with greenhouse gas (GHG) concentration from the IS95 emission scenarios in 1997. Results of the initial study are presented in “Potential Impacts of Climate Change on World Food Supply: Data Sets from a Major Crop Modeling Study,” released by the NASA Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) in 2001. The co-authors developed and tested a method for investigating the spatial implications of climate change on crop production. The Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer dynamic process crop growth models were specified and validated for 127 sites in the major world agricultural regions. Results from the crop models, calibrated and validated in the major crop-growing regions, were then used to test functional forms describing the response of yield changes in the climate and environmental conditions as a percent change by country. The baseline year for crop yield changes is the average yield simulated under current climate (1970-2000 baseline). The resulting yield change data was then fed into trade models to assess impacts on prices and overall food production. Optimal yield is the potential yield not limited by water or fertilizer and without management constraints. Adapted yields are evaluated in each country as a fraction of the potential yield. The weighting factor combines the ratio of current yields to current yield potential and the economic limitation of the economic country’s agricultural systems. This updated version is based on HadCM3 model output along with GHG concentrations from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES). The crop yield estimates incorporate some major improvements: (1) consistent crop simulation methodology and climate change scenarios; (2) weighting of model site results by contribution to regional and national, and rainfed and irrigated, production; (3) quantitative foundation for estimation of physiological CO₂ effects on crop yields; (4) explicit consideration of adaptation; and (5) reporting of results by country rather than by Basic Linked System region. For full documentation, please read the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959378003000827?via%3Dihub). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data is available from the data provider for the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The Climate Change Impacts on Crop Production dataset is a tabular dataset released by NASA SEDAC in collaboration with the NASA GISS. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: ### Overview This dataset details global potential evapotranspiration of a reference crop at 30 arc-seconds resolution (approximately 1km at the equator) for the 1970-2000 period. Evapotranspiration is the simultaneous process of evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation is the process in which liquid water is converted to water vapor. Transpiration is when plants take up water with their roots and release water vapor to the atmosphere through stomata in their leaves. The unit for evapotranspiration is total millimeters (mm) per year. A higher value in mm suggests more water is lost from that cropped surface. Potential evapotranspiration measures the ability of the atmosphere to remove water through evapotranspiration. In this dataset crop evapotranspiration (ET₀) is used as a measure of the evapotranspiration rate from a referenced and standardized vegetated surface (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nation ([FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/X0490E/x0490e04.htm)). This concept of ET₀ is useful to study evaporative demand of the atmosphere in relation to climatic factors and independently of crop type, crop development, and management practices. This dataset was developed by Antonio Trabucco and Robert Zomer with the support of the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI). The dataset can be used to support studies on sustainable development, poverty alleviation, and climate change adaptation. It is particularly relevant to crop and yield modeling and studying the impacts of climate change on future crop production. ### Methodology The widely-used standard equation to estimate potential evapotranspiration is the FAO Penman-Monteith equation (FAO-PM). Researchers used the FAO-PM equation in combination with data on multiple climate variables to produce an estimated ET₀ for a reference crop (well-watered grass at 12 cm of height). A reference crop was used to ensure the final results provided ET₀ information solely based on climate information of a region. Climate data was collected from [WorldClim 2.0 dataset](http://worldclim.org/version2). The World Clim 2.0 dataset includes monthly data on temperature, solar radiation, wind speed and water vapor pressure. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://figshare.com/articles/Global_Aridity_Index_and_Potential_Evapotranspiration_ET0_Climate_Database_v2/7504448/3). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [aridity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli030-Land-Aridity) data from the data provider. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly averaged potential evapotranspiration is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Historical Cyclone Intensity dataset estimates the maximum tropical storm intensity experienced at each point around the globe between 1970 and 2009, as indicated by wind speed. Intensity is described via the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale, meaning each value represents the "strongest" cyclone within each 1 arc minute grid cell during that time. Hurricane‐force winds can destroy buildings and fling dangerous debris. However, storm surge and large waves produced by hurricanes pose the greatest threat to life and property along the coast. A storm surge is an abnormal rise of water generated by a storm's winds.The destructive power of storm surge and large battering waves can result in loss of life, buildings destroyed, beach and dune erosion, and road and bridge damage along the coast. Storm surge can span hundreds of miles of coastland and can travel several miles inland. In estuaries and bayous, salt water intrusion endangers public health and the environment. More powerful storms can lead to stronger winds and larger surges. Tracking historical cyclone events can help in estimating the level of threat posed by storms in a given region. Observations of historical cyclone events are sparse globally, which led researchers to estimate storm characteristics using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2). These modeled results are based primarily on [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01—the most complete global set of historical tropical cyclones available—but United Nations Environment Programme/Global Resource Information Database-Geneva(UNEP/GRID-Geneva) reconciled a wide range of datasets into a common framework. By applying modeling equations to this unified historical archive, UNEP/GRID-Geneva built a homogeneous structured cyclone database with first level basic meteorological data and spatial data. This global cyclone database makes possible post-analysis of historical cyclone events, such as the dataset presented here. ### Methodology This dataset is derived from a geospatial database of historical tropical storms, which includes estimates of wind speeds and other properties across space and time. This database drew upon [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01 as well as tropical cyclone data from Regional Specialised Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) and the Tropical Cyclone Warning Centres (TCWCs) of the World Meteorological Organisation. This database was constructed using the [Cyclone Database Manager](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.117.6313&rep=rep1&type=pdf) created by UNEP/DEWA/GRID-Geneva. Geospatially complete characterizations of historical tropical storms were extrapolated from historical observations using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2), which was selected on the basis of universal recommendation from all polled tropical cyclone specialists. The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). description: ### Overview The Saltmarshes dataset displays the distribution of saltmarshes globally, drawing from occurrence data (surveyed and/or remotely sensed). The dataset captures location data for saltmarsh in 99 countries worldwide. The data were collected from 1973 to 2015, with most occurring after 2005. Saltmarshes are highly productive ecosystems that are rich in biodiversity and underpin the estuarine food web. In particular, saltmarshes serve as nesting, nursery and feeding grounds for numerous species of birds, fish, molluscs and crustaceans. Saltmarshes are extremely valuable but often overlooked ecosystems, contributing to livelihoods locally and globally through the associated ecosystem services they provide, including fish production, carbon storage, and coastal protection. Despite their importance, saltmarsh areas are declining around the world, having lost between 25% and 50% of their global historical coverage ([Crooks et al. 2011](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/18318/605780REPLACEM10of0Coastal0Wetlands.pdf), [Duarte et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12237-008-9038-7)). Vast areas have been lost through conversion to agriculture, urban and industrial land, while remaining saltmarshes face many other current and potential threats ([Gedan et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163930)). In light of increasing anthropogenic and environmental pressures on coastal ecosystems, global data on the occurrence and extent of saltmarshes are needed to draw attention to these critical ecosystems and the benefits they generate for people. The dataset was developed to establish a mapped baseline inventory of the extent of the global distribution of saltmarshes. The data aim to support resource management, strengthen decision-making, and facilitate tracking of progress towards global conservation targets set by multilateral environmental agreements. The UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) collated and integrated the dataset with support from Conservation International and The Nature Conservancy. ### Methodology The Saltmarshes dataset consists of data derived from peer-reviewed articles and [grey literature](https://www.greylit.org/about), including reports and databases created by governmental and non-governmental organisations, universities, institutes and researchers globally. Data in the original source materials were collected using remote sensing and field-based survey methods. Data quality ranges from high-resolution maps to low-resolution representations, with the scale varying from 1:10,000 to 1:4,000,000, with most falling within the 1:10,000 to 1:100,000 range. Data contributors were asked to submit metadata with each dataset to provide the contextual information important for informing analyses. Saltmarshes were identified in accordance with definitions provided by data sources, where available, or were determined using expert opinion (available in the supplementary material).The precautionary principle was applied to ensure consistency across designations: if the authors were uncertain about the classification of the habitat, it was not included. Please refer to the supplementary material and associated [metadata](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/pdfs/43/WCMC_027_Global_Distribution_of_Saltmarsh.pdf?1617122640) from the authors for more information regarding each data source presented. For the full documentation, please see the source [publication](https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.5.e11764). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. It is composed of numerical ratings and supporting descriptive texts for 195 countries and 14 territories. Freedom in the World has been published since 1973, allowing Freedom House to track global trends in freedom over more than 40 years. External analysts assess the 209 countries and territories using a combination of on-the-ground research, consultations with local contacts, and information from news articles, nongovernmental organizations, governments, and a variety of other sources. Expert advisers and regional specialists then vet the analysts’ conclusions. The final product represents the consensus of the analysts, advisers, and Freedom House staff. For each country and territory, Freedom in the World analyzes the electoral process, political pluralism and participation, the functioning of the government, freedom of expression and of belief, associational and organizational rights, the rule of law, and personal autonomy and individual rights. A country or territory is assigned 2 ratings (7 to 1)—one for political rights and one for civil liberties—based on its total scores for the political rights and civil liberties questions. Each rating of 1 through 7, with 1 representing the greatest degree of freedom and 7 the smallest degree of freedom, corresponds to a specific range of total scores. The average of a country’s or territory’s political rights and civil liberties ratings is called the Freedom Rating, and it is this figure that determines the status of free (1.0 to 2.5), partly free (3.0 to 5.0), or not free (5.5 to 7.0). description: Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,400 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: The Change in Snowmelt Timing, 1975-2040, by Freshwater Ecoregion data set from the Nature Conservancy was developed by summarizing weekly averages of snowmelt for each 0.5-degree cell. Weekly snowmelt averages were derived using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) macroscale hydrologic model, which simulates spatially distributed total runoff and snowmelt over all global land areas for two time periods (past period covers 1961-1990; future period, 2025-2054). These modeled data were provided by the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Washington in Seattle and Washington State University in Pullman. The change in snowmelt peak is represented as the number of weeks' difference between past peak week and future peak week for each 0.5-degree cell and then averaged these values across each ecoregion. Areas where past snow cover was consistently absent over a ten-year period were excluded by using a snow cover mask derived from the 0.5-degree Nimbus-7 SMMR satellite data. Areas where peak snowmelt varied little throughout the averaged year were also excluded by using a mask of cells greater than one standard deviation of the past peak snowmelt range. The Upper Amur River (Shilka) has very high results largely due to extreme decadal shifts in precipitation. Local peak time shifts within ecoregions can be longer than this summarized map relates. It assesses the REGIO-OECD “degree of urbanization” model using as input the population grid cells in 4 epochs (2015, 2000, 1990, and 1975). Each km2 grid cell has been generated by integration of built-up areas produced from Landsat image and population data derived from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (CIESIN GPW v4). These data are divided into 3 discrete categories: urban centers, urban cluster, and rural areas. Urban centers, or high density clusters, are defined as “contiguous cells (4-connectivity, gap filling) with a density of at least 1,500 inhabitants/km² or a density of built-up greater than 50%, and a minimum of 50,000 inhabitants” per cluster. Urban clusters are lower-density clusters including towns and suburbs, defined as contiguous grid cells with a population of at least 300 inhabitants per km² or a density of built-up greater than 50% and a minimum of 5,000 inhabitants. Rural areas are defined as grid cells outside high-density clusters and urban clusters. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) created a 250 m resolution population grid. Residential population estimates for 1975, 1990, 2000, and 2015 were disaggregated from census or administrative units to grid cells, informed by the distribution and density of built-up (BU) as mapped in the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) global layer per corresponding epoch. To produce the new population grids, a simple model was developed and implemented. The approach was based on raster-based dasymetric mapping relying on GHS-BUILT as a proxy to restrict and refine the distribution of people and inform on the respective density. The BU grid is the distribution of BU areas expressed as their proportion of occupied footprint in each cell. Population estimates consisted of country-based layers of census and administrative polygons containing estimated residential population for target years. For each period, population grids were produced following a clear volume-preserving dasymetric mapping approach: given a consensus layer and a GHSL BU raster layer, for a populated polygon (source zone), (a) if the polygon generates 250 m cells and contains BU area, disaggregate the population in proportion to density of BU; (b) if the polygon generates 250 m cells and does not contain BU, disaggregate population using areal weighting; (c) if the polygon does not generate its own 250 m cell, convert polygon to point (centroid within), sum all points within a cell, and sum to a mosaic of (a) and (b). Option (c) was required because some populated source zones (polygons) were smaller than a 250 x 250 m cell. This model preserved the full resolution of the Gridded Population of the World (GPW) input population units and conserved the total input population. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set.
